slides.speaker_notes:
[0:00 - 0:15 | Slide 1: Introduction · 32 words]
Judges, this is ReturnLens. For solo online sellers, returns are overwhelming. ReturnLens unifies buyer claims, video evidence, and store rules into one clear decision pack. The model observes, code verifies, but the seller always decides.

slides.decision_question: THE SELLER'S QUESTION: Packing mistake, delivery error, or unboxing swap? The seller needs verified facts before deciding to refund, replace, or inspect.
slides.speaker_notes:
[0:15 - 0:40 | Slide 2: The Problem · 58 words]
A customer chats in: 'I ordered white headphones, but received black. Please refund me,' attaching an unboxing clip. The merchant has to check four tabs: chat, Shopify, tracking, and store policy. Was this a warehouse mix-up, an honest confusion, or a swap? Blind refunds erode margins, while blind rejections destroy trust. The merchant needs unified facts to choose the next step.

slides.disclaimer: * Illustrative concept scenario with staged mock evidence.
slides.speaker_notes:
[0:40 - 1:25 | Slide 3: The Core Demonstration · 98 words]
Here is our core demonstration. The Shopify order specifies white headphones, but the customer's video shows black casing. ReturnLens flags this visible difference clearly. Notice our honest AI grounding: we state that the barcode and exact model are unverified from the video frame. We do not jump to calling this fraud—it could easily be a warehouse packing error. Instead, ReturnLens prepares three practical options for the seller. Notice option two: a drafted reply is already written, asking for the outer-box label to verify the shipment. The seller simply reviews and clicks to send.

slides.title: Models observe. Code verifies. Seller authorizes.
slides.subtitle: A structured agent pipeline that investigates, checks policies, and drafts the next step.

pipeline_steps.desc: Ingests customer chat, tracking scan, and extracts cited video keyframes.
Cross-checks observed color against catalog specs, delivery date, and 7-day policy.
Synthesizes matches and discrepancies into 3 actionable choices and drafts replies.
Human merchant reviews the evidence pack and clicks one button to confirm.

clarification_loop.title: DYNAMIC CLARIFICATION (CASE C):
clarification_loop.flow: Unclear evidence → Request a close-up photo → Add to same case file → Continue review
clarification_loop.desc: If footage is dark or blurry, agent requests 1 close-up photo or box label and continues the same case. Never auto-rejects.

slides.responsibility_line: Models observe visual traits · Code checks dates and policy rules · Seller authorizes all actions
slides.speaker_notes:
[1:25 - 2:05 | Slide 4: Agent Behavior · 88 words]
How does the agent move the case forward? It follows four stages: First, Collect—ingesting chat, tracking data, and keyframes. Second, Compare—deterministic code verifies the seven-day return window and checks color alignment. Third, Recommend—the agent drafts resolution choices and customer replies. And fourth, Seller Decides—the merchant makes the call. If footage is too dark or blurry, the agent requests a clear close-up photo, appends it to the same case file, and resumes review. Models observe, code checks rules, and the seller authorizes.

columns.seller_outcome: Customer gets a fair chance to clarify. If 2nd attempt fails, escalates directly to seller.

slides.speaker_notes:
[2:05 - 2:30 | Slide 5: Three Scenarios · 54 words]
Our prototype focuses on three everyday situations: In Case A, evidence is clean—a visible crack on arrival within seven days. The agent drafts a return label. In Case B, color discrepancy—the agent surfaces the conflict and prepares choices. In Case C, unclear evidence—the agent requests a close-up photo. Each scenario produces a clear next step.

[2:30 - 3:00 | Slide 6: Execution Roadmap & Closing · 50 words]
For this 24-hour hackathon, our scope is strictly disciplined: Person A builds the state machine and policy checks; Person B builds the keyframe viewer and merchant console; Person C tests all three scenarios. We are not building live Shopify webhooks or banking integrations. One clear evidence pack. The seller makes the call. Thank you!

qa_defense.question: Why do you need an agent instead of a simple form or rules engine?
qa_defense.answer: A standard rules engine can only check structured database fields like dates. It cannot inspect unboxing video keyframes, identify product colors, handle customer clarification dialogues, or synthesize contradictory evidence into a coherent decision pack. The agent bridges messy multimodal customer input with strict merchant policies.

qa_defense.question: Why doesn't a color discrepancy prove customer fraud?
qa_defense.answer: A color discrepancy only indicates that the product in the video differs from the Shopify order. It could easily be a warehouse shipping mistake, an order fulfillment mix-up, or the customer opening a family member's parcel by mistake. Accusing the customer of fraud destroys goodwill; presenting choices lets the merchant decide based on their knowledge of their warehouse accuracy.

qa_defense.question: What happens when unboxing video footage is dark, blurry, or inconclusive?
qa_defense.answer: In Case C, customers cannot re-film an unboxing once opened. ReturnLens requests a clear close-up photo or outer-box shipping label. The agent appends this new evidence to the existing case file, retaining the original video. If a second attempt still fails, it escalates directly to the merchant with the full dossier.

qa_defense.question: What authority does the merchant retain in this system?
qa_defense.answer: The merchant retains 100% decision authority. ReturnLens is strictly fail-closed: it has zero authority to issue payments, trigger chargebacks, or send rejection notices on its own. It prepares drafted return options and drafted messages, but every consequential action requires a one-click merchant confirmation.

qa_defense.question: What does your 24-hour prototype actually prove?
qa_defense.answer: Our 24-hour prototype proves the end-to-end feasibility of multimodal return triage: extracting keyframes, running deterministic rule checks, handling a dynamic clarification loop, and generating an actionable decision console for the seller across three realistic benchmark scenarios.
